learning: Iteration 1 changed span and kp together, so its result cannot be attributed to either. Compare this race against iteration 1 with the kp change in mind. If line loss stays at 1.0 or more on the slalom, the next test is wider pitch (20 mm) rather than more gain.
notes: Complete package for the Builder's 16 mm contiguous seven-sensor layout. Weights stay proportional to x and kp rises to 5.0 to hold steering gain as the sensor span widens; the controller change is reported separately.
rationale: Iteration 0 (five 12 mm sensors, span ±0.024 m) and iteration 1 (seven 12 mm sensors, span ±0.036 m) both lost the line about once per run on the s-bend and slalom, with max_error at 0.060 to 0.067 m, just past the 0.06 m off-track limit. Iteration 1 also changed kp from 3.0 to 4.0 and flattened the weights, so its score drop (64.7 to 50.7) cannot be attributed to span alone. The Builder's new proposal keeps seven sensors but moves to 16 mm footprints at 16 mm pitch (x = ±0.048 m, y = 0.03 m), which tiles the span contiguously and extends the outer edge. I keep the geometry exactly as proposed. For the controller, I keep weights proportional to x, scaled so the outer sensors are ±1.0, which matches the contract's requirement that a positive signal steers left for positive x. The wider footprint lengthens the lateral distance over which the signal moves from -1 to +1, so the effective steering gain per metre of error falls. Iteration 0 gave roughly 125 per metre (kp 3.0 over a 0.024 m weight scale), and iteration 1 gave roughly 111 per metre. Holding about 104 per metre at the new 0.048 m scale needs kp near 5.0, so I set kp to 5.0. I keep ki 0.05, kd 0.3, base_speed 1.5 and line_loss 'last_direction' unchanged, since iteration 0 and 1 gave no evidence that they limit the result. Expected result: line_loss_events near zero on the s-bend and slalom, max_error below 0.06 m, and at least some completions. Because kp changed along with the geometry, the race result mixes both effects; I report the controller change so the next iteration can separate them.
